title: Sidney Bechet as a boy and his return
summary: Bechet grew up near Laurent, began on a cheap flute, played for a dollar a night, and later sold tunes for whiskey; Laurent met him at the airport.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: I was going to ask about Sidney Bechet, if you heard him when you were a boy, he wasn't much older.

Sidney brought up right by my house all these days. About the same age as you? He's just a few years older than me. He must have been around about four years older than me. But Sidney left here, when Sidney left here, and he didn't get back here in twenty some odd years. When Sidney got back here, I'm the man, picked Sidney and his manager up at the airport in my car. And I had a layout for him that night up at the house with him and his manager. I gave him a party that night.
In the late years he played the soprano sax more than he did clarinet. Than he did clarinet. Did he play clarinet mostly here or the other?

Well he was brought up on the clarinet more than the soprano. He picked the soprano up afterwards. He was great on the clarinet. Well he played a flute first, a little fifteen cents flute, six-hole flute. That's why he learned to play, on a little fifteen cents flute. He played that flute so well they gave him a clarinet. They gave him one. And he played the clarinet so well, until Pete Lawley used to hire him out there for a dollar a night to play on Iberville, Murray, that night. He played up there in short pants. He played up there. A dollar a night.
Was he really good in those days when he was a boy?

He was good. He was good. He was good. Well I'm telling you, he left here, he didn't have a music warning in his head when he left here. Then when Teor and them, Peter and them came back from Teor, he told me, he said, man sitting is up there writing numbers and composing numbers for a bottle of whiskey. Some of them fellas would come there and put them two-fifth whiskey on the table and tell him- Yeah, that's a company sure somebody- Says, man, pick up that soprano, let me hear you knock that number. And he knocked that number and they taped that number on him. He was selling them numbers for five dollars, Lorenzo told me. Five dollars. A bottle of whiskey. Gang of numbers he cut. This is his last number of your- Well, this one first. Let's see.
